title: A tridimensional model of AI literacy: An empirical analysis of student performance and demographic patterns in higher education
keywords: AI literacy|artificial intelligence in education|undergraduate students|gender differences|academic stage|technological literacy|differentiated instruction|AI literacy assessment|higher education|AI ethics education
abstract: This study moves beyond theoretical frameworks to empirically analyse artificial intelligence (AI) literacy among undergraduate students, identifying distinct performance profiles to inform educational interventions. Using a validated, performance-based instrument, we assessed the functional, technical and socio-critical competencies of 353 students at a private university in Mexico. Our analysis revealed three distinct student profiles: lower performance (n = 85), mid-range proficiency (n = 158) and higher competence (n = 107). A critical finding across all profiles was a significant deficit in the socio-critical dimension, with only 2.6% of students demonstrating outstanding ability. Furthermore, the profiles varied significantly by gender and academic stage, challenging traditional assumptions about technology literacy. These findings provide an evidence-based typology for diagnosing student needs and developing targeted, equitable educational strategies to foster comprehensive AI literacy in higher education. Implications for practice or policy: Curriculum leaders should view AI literacy as a transversal competence, integrating ethical and critical reflection across curricula. Educators and instructional designers must apply differentiated instruction based on learner profiles, recognising that AI literacy development is complex and challenges assumptions about gender and academic progression. Policymakers should promote validated assessment tools to replace anecdotal evidence with empirical data, guiding institutional strategies and resource allocation for AI education.

title: Igniting the future of cardiovascular care: highlights from the ESC Digital and AI Summit 2025 in Berlin
topic: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
keywords: digital health|large language models|foundation models|clinical decision support|AI agents|diagnostic reasoning|clinical implementation of AI|AI literacy|AI adoption barriers|cardiology education
abstract: The ESC, as a leading authority in cardiovascular education, guidelines, and resources for the international cardiology community, acknowledges the strategic significance of digital health and therefore called for the organization of the first ESC Digital and AI Summit, which was held in Berlin in 21–22 November, 2025. The Summit articulated a clear ambition: move beyond proof-of-concept and early-stage research toward clinical implementation of AI and digital health in cardiovascular care. As highlighted by Summit leadership, the majority of existing work remains in early validation—the Summit’s aim is to define the ‘final frontier’: safe, effective, ethical deployment in real-world cardiovascular care. With more than 800 participants from 63 countries, it achieved its mission to build a cross-disciplinary community with a focus on cardiovascular health, combining clinicians, engineers, data scientists, patient advocates and industry to co-design solutions, establish best practices, promote digital and AI literacy, and identify practical barriers to adoption. With a total of 33 scientific sessions, 11 symposia, 1 debate, 2 How to sessions, 3 Roundtable sessions and 1 interactive voting session, the event offered a versatile programme to the participants from all fields and levels of expertise. Start-ups and academic developers could pitch their innovation on the Digital Stage and live demonstrate their innovations in the dedicated Technology and Innovation Demo Room. From the submissions received for this specific track, 33 innovations were selected and shown. Two winners were finally awarded for early developments and more advanced products. The scientific programme was complemented by the presentation of 179 abstracts either shown in the dedicated ‘Advances in Science’ session on the Digital Stage, as moderated ePosters or printed Posters. The two keynote sessions and the debate provided a comprehensive view on the impact of Foundation models and Large Language Models (LLMs) in cardiovascular care. ESC pioneers this development by releasing a dedicated ESC Chabot that was fine-tuned on existing guidelines, providing physicians the opportunity to align their treatment decisions with the current guidelines. However, it was demonstrated that benchmarking such models with exam-style questions—for example, those used in the United States Medical Licensing Examination—does not reflect clinical reality. In practice, the correct diagnosis is gradually narrowed down by comparing different possible diseases that may cause similar symptoms. Diagnostic tests are requested and performed accordingly. Current AI systems significantly simplify this process. AI Agents orchestrating such different stages of tasks show promising first results, however, LLMs, often the core of such an orchestration mechanism, currently remain too sensitive to order and length of input instructions leading to wrong conclusions. Human-AI collaboration therefore remains imperative in this process, navigating the trade-offs between human deskilling and expert-driven analysis that relies on an AI as a second check, a ‘co-pilot’. Dedicated cardiovascular AI tools hold great promise for the much-needed further optimization of our cardiovascular clinical workflows. However, this requires stringent precautions for responsible clinical implementation. Compliance with the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and the upcoming European AI Act, among other things, necessitates rigorous validation and continuous post-market surveillance. Furthermore, widespread adoption of AI tools requires addressing several critical points of concern. These include, among others, mapping out clear clinical workflows, ensuring high-quality interoperable data, building clinical trust through education, robust ethical governance, and, importantly, sustainable reimbursement models. These complex challenges were intensively discussed during the Summit at various roundtables, where cardiologists, scientists, patients, industry partners, politicians, and regulators came together. This collaborative effort underscores the multi-stakeholder commitment required to transform CV AI from promising innovations into an integral part of cardiovascular care in Europe and beyond. Although AI-enabled workflows are enhancing clinical practice, achieving safe and reliable implementation remains a major hurdle. Digital health is reshaping the responsibilities of healthcare professionals, redefining patient–physician interactions, and placing greater emphasis on shared decision-making and encouraging individuals to assume greater responsibility for their own health. Meaningful and sustained transformation arises when individuals actively engage in managing their health, supported by clinicians in the role of trusted partners. This paradigm shift highlights the imperative to adequately prepare the next generation of healthcare professionals to navigate and excel within this evolving healthcare landscape. Patient representatives actively engaged in the discussions around these topics at the Summit, making the event an opportunity where the voices of patients are heard. One of the jointly organized sessions with the European Association of Cardiothoracic Surgery (EACTS) offered a forward-looking exploration of emerging technologies in surgical practice. The session covered advances in robotics and telesurgery, emphasizing the critical need for modern high-performance network infrastructures—such as 5G and future 6G systems—to ensure low-latency, reliable remote interventions. In addition, the discussion highlighted the growing role of virtual and augmented reality as sophisticated planning tools that enable surgeons to rehearse complex procedures, improve spatial understanding, and enhance preoperative preparation. Together, these innovations illustrate how digital and networked technologies are reshaping cardiothoracic surgery and setting new standards for precision, safety, and procedural efficiency. As Europe’s largest and most dynamic startup ecosystem, Berlin attracted top AI talent, digital health entrepreneurs, and investors, creating fertile ground for showcasing and accelerating new cardiovascular technologies. Next year's event will take place in Basel, Switzerland. The region’s academic strengths, particularly through institutions such as the University of Basel, ETH Zürich, and nearby Swiss and German university hospitals, ensure access to cutting-edge research in cardiology, imaging, bioengineering, and machine learning, enabling deep scientific exchange and opportunities to showcase translational work with real clinical impact. Furthermore, the vibrant region offers branches of major AI tech and Pharmaceutical companies, and the leading ELLIS Europe site Cybervalley in Tübingen, Strasbourg with its excellence centre in Surgical Data Science and Tuttlingen as a major MedTech area closed by. Switzerland’s innovation-friendly regulatory landscape further strengthens the case for Basel, as the country is known for progressive approaches to digital health, robust data privacy frameworks, and strong intellectual property protection, which are critical factors for fostering trust in AI-enabled medical technologies. The program organization of the Summit is one core responsibility of the Digital Cardiology and AI (DCAI) Committee for building an ecosystem of pioneers, start-ups, experts, industry, clinicians, and policymakers collaborating to disseminate cutting-edge content throughout the ESC community, promoting evidence-based decision-making. This mission will be continued in Basel in 2026. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

title: Dilemmas of AI-assisted linguistic upbringing – researching preferences and fears of student teachers of foreign languages and home language
keywords: artificial intelligence in education|pre-service teachers|generative AI|ethical use of AI|teacher education curriculum|foreign language teacher training|teacher attitudes toward AI
abstract: With Artificial Intelligence revolutionizing every single aspect of life, it is no wonder that education will also be transformed. Teachers are facing the challenges of becoming familiar with and understanding new tools and incorporating them into their instruction and upbringing. The purpose of the study was to investigate future teachers’ preferences and fears about AI-assisted education and upbringing, with a special focus on ethical aspects of AI use. Since the concept of linguistic upbringing, understood as supporting humans in putting their potential into action, is gaining more prominence these days, it is essential to see the ethical side of the teachers’ relationship with Artificial Intelligence. To address these issues, an anonymous questionnaire was conducted among student teachers of foreign languages and Polish in a number of universities all over Poland. The research showed student teachers’ well-established beliefs in the role of Generative AI in education as well as their high level of awareness of dangers and problems posed by AI. The article proposed recommendations for enriching teacher preparation programs with topics related to AI in a dispersed way.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a supporting factor for the modern teacher: Threats, benefits, and opportunities
keywords: artificial intelligence in education|teachers|AI tools in teaching|teacher stress|teacher-student relationship|teacher workload|educational technology
abstract: The article, against the background of considerations devoted to the changes in the modern world, presents selected areas of application of tools based on artificial intelligence (AI) in the everyday work of teachers. After discussing examples of the threats resulting from the use of AI in the school environment, it presents – divided into thematic categories – the basic possibilities of using AI by teachers to optimize and improve the process of carrying out their daily professional duties. Attention was paid to the resulting indirect benefits, with particular emphasis on reducing the level of occupational stress they experience and increasing the time they devote to students, leading, among other things, to strengthening of the relationship between them.

title: Students of pedagogy and artificial intelligence - attitudes and selected relationships
keywords: attitudes toward AI|pedagogy students|pre-service teachers|early childhood education|AI knowledge|AI acceptance|technology acceptance|artificial intelligence in education|cross-cultural comparison
abstract: Education, understood as upbringing in the broadest and most comprehensive sense, is currently an area of potentially high absorption of AI technologies. Attitudes towards it are among the factors that determine the effectiveness of its implementation. This paper presents an analysis of the attitudes of students of pedagogy and pre-school and early school education (n=304) towards artificial intelligence and their selected dependencies. For the purposes of the project, the Artificial Intelligence online survey questionnaire conducted in March 2024 among a representative sample of adult US citizens (n=1,100) was translated and then adapted to the attitude survey. The actions taken resulted in both an accurate and reliable tool, in line with the assumed theoretical model, and the possibility of contextualizing the discussion of the results in the context of data obtained from a group of young Americans of an age appropriate for the students surveyed. Students of pedagogy represent conservative and rather low (negative) attitudes towards artificial intelligence, differing significantly from their peers in the United States. Particularly noteworthy is the significant and directly proportional relationship between the level of attitude and the declared knowledge of AI, especially with regard to the behavioural component. The resulting image, quite far from expectations, is consistent with some of the reports published in this field, complementing the collage of differently shaped attitudes towards the latest technologies.

title: The application of artificial intelligence in the education of people with disabilities – a pedagogical and philosophical perspective
keywords: artificial intelligence in education|people with disabilities|cognitive enhancement|extended mind|posthumanism|prosthetics|assistive technology|inclusion|philosophy of education|pedagogy
abstract: The subject of the article is the issue of using tools equipped with artificial intelligence (AI) technology in the education of people with disabilities. The conceptual framework will be, on the one hand, contemporary tendencies in the humanities to raise the importance of the role of non-human (posthuman) actors (agents) in networks of agency. On the other hand, the concepts of the extended cognitive system are present in contemporary epistemology. The use of AI tools in education will be analyzed from the perspective of cognitive enhancements. In particular, the analyses will concern the validity of their use, taking into account the dynamic development of AI applications in various areas of social life, including education, for which the dissemination of AI is a challenge. The aim of the article will be to consider the validity of using this type of cognitive enhancement in the education of people with disabilities. Possible (both positive and negative) consequences of such actions will be analyzed. In particular, in addition to the concepts of assistive technology and common technology that appear in the literature, the concept of prosthetic technology will be proposed, which may be helpful when considering the inclusion of specific tools (including those equipped with AI) in the education process. The considerations will be conducted from both pedagogical and philosophical perspectives.

title: Th e illusion of upbringing in the school entering the era of generative AI
keywords: generative AI in education|upbringing|personal formation|Vygotsky|Axel Honneth|simulation|proceduralism|depersonalization|teacher attitudes toward AI|algorithm optimization|secondary schools|educational policy discourse
abstract: This article examines the integration of generative AI (GenAI) into contemporary schooling through the lens of upbringing—understood as a relational, dialogical, and ethical process of personal formation. Drawing on Maria Dudzikowa’s concept of the illusion of education’s formative function, along with Lev Vygotsky’s and Axel Honneth’s theories, it argues that AI does not transform schooling’s formative mission but deepens patterns of simulation, proceduralism, and depersonalization. Based on ethnographic research in two Polish secondary schools (2022–2024) and critical discourse analysis of national policy and educational media, the study reveals a widening gap between official GenAI narratives and everyday school practices. Fieldwork shows students using AI covertly to meet formal requirements, while teachers often ignore or discredit such tools—reinforcing compliance over relational engagement. The article conceptualizes AI as a technological intensifier of schooling rituals, enabling simulation without recognition or dialogue, and calls for renewed pedagogical commitment to relationships and ethical presence in an age of algorithmic optimization.

title: Studying the GenAI’s Impact on Learning and Critical Thinking: A Multi-Site Field Experiment
source_name: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
keywords: generative AI in education|ChatGPT|critical thinking|higher education|AI-assisted learning|student motivation|prompt engineering|content understanding|originality
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are transforming higher education, but robust evidence of their pedagogical value is limited. This multi-site field experiment, based on Situated Cognition Theory, explores the impact of GenAI on learning and critical thinking at ten universities and polytechnics. Around 270 students were randomly assigned to an experimental group using licensed ChatGPT for a supervised task, or a control group using traditional resources. Tasks, aligned with local learning outcomes, were evaluated using a rubric assessing critical thinking, accuracy, coherence, and originality. Classroom observations and a post-task questionnaire further enriched the analysis. Preliminary results indicate that ChatGPT enhanced content comprehension and motivation, but many students struggled with evaluating AI reliability and creating effective prompts.

title: Using ChatGPT to Create Therapeutic Fairy Tales for Students with Psychosocial Difficulties
keywords: ChatGPT|artificial intelligence in education|psychosocial problems|special education teachers|elementary school students|emotional and behavioral problems|adaptive challenges|relationship problems|school-based treatment|teacher experiences
abstract: The aim of this study was to explore the experiences of special education teachers in using personalized therapeutic stories generated by artificial intelligence (specifically ChatGPT) in their work with students in grades IV–VI of primary school who exhibit psychosocial difficulties. The research employed a qualitative approach and was conducted using in-depth interviews with teachers working with students facing emotional, relational, and adaptive challenges. The findings indicate that teachers see great potential in this tool, particularly in terms of content personalization and engaging students in the process of change. The conclusions drawn from this study may serve as a foundation for further research on the use of ChatGPT in pedagogy and contribute to the development of educational and therapeutic materials that support the work of teachers and school-based therapists.

title: Teacher professionalization and professionalism in the context of contemporary challenges of the age of artificial intelligence
keywords: teacher professionalization|teacher professionalism|artificial intelligence in education|sociology of work|Andrew Abbott|teaching profession
abstract: The article presents a theoretical analysis of the literature in the field of sociology of work (by English-speaking authors) and pedeutology, focusing on the issue of professionalization and professionalism. The aim of the article is to explore the current state of teacher professionalization and professionalism, with a particular focus on the challenges introduced by artificial intelligence. At the outset of the article, the clarification of key terms was considered essential for the considerations undertaken. As the theoretical framework for evaluating teacher professionalization and professionalism, classical theories of the sociology of work and Andrew Abbott’s concept were taken into account. In conclusion, the discussion returns to the work of the teacher, taking into account the development of artificial intelligence and the aspect of teacher professionalism. Based on a review of the selected literature, a conclusion was also formulated regarding the question of whether it is justified to classify teaching as a profession.

title: Network bans vs. ministerial guidance: press narratives on ChatGPT in education (U.S./Poland)
keywords: ChatGPT|generative AI in education|press framing|media narratives|AI policy|teacher professional development|assessment redesign|policy styles|AI risk management|United States|Poland
abstract: This article uses Critical Discourse Analysis and Framing Analysis to compare how the press in the United States and Poland framed the educational use of ChatGPT during November 30, 2022–November 30, 2023. A small, purposefully selected corpus of critical and contrasting cases (NYC ban vs ministerial guidance) was coded for dominant frames, topic foci, and stances. Four patterns emerge: (1) a trigger asymmetry—a network-level ban anchors the U.S. storyline, while ministerial guidance and risk-management language (monitoring, vigilance, plagiarism tools) shape the Polish one; (2) movement from restriction to management, with Polish items foregrounding capacity gaps (training, workload, infrastructure); (3) conditional opportunity frames in both contexts, dependent on competence, policy clarity, and assessment redesign; and (4) different distributions of actors and responsibility (district decision-making vs teacher vigilance and guidance compliance). The analysis suggests that policy style channels the debate either toward permission vs prohibition (U.S.) or toward capability building and risk management (Poland). Implications include prioritising targeted teacher development, redesigning assessment to value process evidence, and adopting school-level protocols aligned with national guidance. Scope note: findings map discursive patterns in selected outlets and do not estimate prevalence does not yet appear fully prepared.

title: Pedagogy as a value filter: rethinking education in the age of artifi cial intelligence
keywords: artificial intelligence in education|critical pedagogy|axiology|humanistic education|digital justice|digital access|relationality|dehumanization|future skills|trust|technology and subjectivity|AI ethics
abstract: The aim of this article is to present education as a key category of pedagogical reflection in the face of cultural and ethical challenges posed by artificial intelligence. Education is not viewed here as a mere supplement to digital learning but as a space of axiological resistance to the dominance of technology over relationships, values, and subjectivity. This is a theoretical-reflective paper based on selected literature in critical pedagogy, philosophy of education, and technology studies. The argument is structured around five thematic axes: the redefinition of education in an automated world; digital justice and access; relationality as resistance to dehumanization; future competencies; and trust as a pedagogical category. The article contributes to the debate on the humanistic dimension of education in the age of artificial intelligence and emphasizes the need to consciously shape subjects capable of living with technology, not under it.

title: Teachers’ Technological, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge related to Artificial Intelligence as a Protective Factor Against Technostress and Techno-anxiety
keywords: AI-TPACK|technostress|pedagogical content knowledge|artificial intelligence in education|teacher education curriculum|in-service teachers|moderating effect|protective factors
abstract: The integration of information technology in education, including AI tools, may induce anxiety and serve as a source of significant technostress. A potential mitigating factor for both phenomena is teachers’ technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge related to AI (AI-TPACK). This hypothesis was examined in a cross-sectional, correlational study involving 364 students in teacher training programs and 55 in-service teachers. Data were collected using standardized instruments: the Abbreviated Technology Anxiety Scale (Wilson et al., 2023), the Person-Environment Fit Scale of Technostress (Wang et al., 2020), and the Intelligent Technological, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge Scale (Celik, 2023). Results indicated low levels of techno-anxiety and technostress and moderate levels of AI-TPACK in both groups. As expected, techno-anxiety and technostress were strongly and positively correlated, while both were negatively associated with AI-TPACK. Moreover, AI-TPACK significantly moderated the relationship between techno-anxiety and technostress in selected configurations. The findings are discussed in the context of international literature, highlighting their practical implications.

title: A pedagogically designed bilingers system: towards universal bilingual education in the age of AI
keywords: artificial intelligence in education|generative AI|bilingual education|early childhood education|preschool education|AI recommendation systems|teaching materials|pedagogical foundations|teacher support
abstract: For several years, numerous articles on artificial intelligence (AI) have appeared in scientific journals related to education. This article, which focuses on computer platforms for teachers, parents, and children in preschool and early childhood education, belongs to this group. The authors of the article who prepare educational materials for use on AI platforms focus on linking these materials with the foundations of pedagogy and with the expectations that platforms, teachers, and institutions working with children are expected to meet. The article describes the first step in implementing AI, in which AI is used to recommend appropriate actions for teachers. However, considering the current situation, due to numerous implementations in Poland and abroad, the use of generative AI could be considered to assist in the development of many new materials, the recommendation system proved more effective. The results of this work will be presented in a subsequent publication after the research is completed.

title: The need for educational formation of moral intelligence of youth in the school environment in the era of development of artificial intelligence
keywords: moral intelligence|moral education|youth|adolescents|artificial intelligence|school environment|value system formation|risk-taking|sensation seeking|digital technologies
abstract: Today we live in a time of intensive development of knowledge, digital technology and artificial intelligence. The impact of information and communication development on young people's functioning is increasingly noticeable, especially in the cognitive, linguistic, social and moral areas. During adolescence, young people begin to fulfil developmental tasks, enter new roles and establish their value system. This stage is also characterised by sensation-seeking and engaging in risky behaviour. It should be important during this period of development to take care of the formation of conscious, appropriate attitudes, moral principles and the value system of the young generation. The purpose of this article is to present the issue of moral intelligence and to show the importance of the formation of this type of intelligence in young people by the school environment. It is also important to show the opportunities and threats resulting from the development of artificial intelligence for the functioning of young people. It is also worth looking at the specifics of adolescent development, the possibilities of shaping moral intelligence on an educational level by using traditional methods as well as the achievements of artificial intelligence.

title: Where Is the Little House Headed? – Narratives by Children and Those Generated by AI
keywords: children's narratives|AI-generated stories|ChatGPT|anthropomorphism|narrative agency|moralization|kindergarten children|elementary school students
abstract: The study aims to identify the ways of narrative building based on a selected frame – an illustration from “The Little House” book, authored by Virginia Lee Burton. The performed iconotext analysis initiated an attempt to answer the question of how the story’s protagonist and space elements were constructed (and hence the search for the referenced categories in the narratives analysed for the sake of this publication). The article summarises twenty-five stories authored by children (6–7 years old) and fifty narratives generated with the ChatGPT 4.0 language model. The study was conducted within a qualitative paradigm, using a participatory observation perspective. The material for the study (preceded by an iconotext analysis) was collected during workshops in a kindergarten group in a community primary school and among year one pupils in a public primary school. Both schools operate in a big Polish city (population over 500,000). The analysis revealed a tendency to anthropomorphise the Little House and assign its agency (contradicted with a passive attitude in the original version) – both in children’s narratives and in the language model-generated ones. The differences occurred in the spatial context – children’s narratives were deeply rooted in everyday experiences. AI-generated stories, in turn, were more diversified and schematic, with a tendency to moralisation and philosophical generalisation. The confrontation of children’s narratives with the AI-generated narratives revealed the potential and limitations of the language model, including but not limited to understanding and interpreting the visual nuances.

title: Charting the developmental landscape of artificial intelligence in language education using bibliometric methods
keywords: artificial intelligence in language teaching|second language acquisition|chatbots|generative AI|student engagement|AI acceptance|research trends|co-citation analysis|co-word analysis
abstract: This study investigates the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in language education by conducting a bibliometric analysis to uncover patterns, trends, and gaps in the current body of research. While AI tools such as chatbots, intelligent writing assistants, and generative models are increasingly adopted in second language learning, the field lacks a comprehensive synthesis of scholarly developments. To address this, the study analyzed 837 articles retrieved from the Web of Science using VOSviewer for both co-citation and co-word analyses. The results identified several core thematic areas in the literature, reflecting the convergence of pedagogical strategies, learner outcomes, technological advancement, and user acceptance. Co-citation analysis revealed how foundational works are shaping the field, while co-occurrence of keywords indicated the dominance of themes such as AI-supported instruction, emotional and cognitive engagement, and the adoption of AI frameworks in educational practice. These findings offer a structured conceptual map of AI’s role in language education, revealing a strong alignment between pedagogical research and technological innovation. The study provides theoretical insights into the interdisciplinary convergence of education and AI, while also highlighting the practical need for equitable, teacher-inclusive, and sustainable adoption of AI tools, thereby advancing the broader agenda of inclusive and quality education for all.

title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Language Education: Global Trends and Future Directions
source_name: Journal of Language Literature and Cultural Dynamics
keywords: AI literacy|language teaching|generative AI|AI-assisted language learning|critical AI literacy|teacher readiness|teacher professional development|AI ethics|learner autonomy|responsible AI use|research trends
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed educational practice, particularly in language learning environments where generative AI tools are increasingly used for writing support, feedback, translation, and personalized instruction. Despite this expansion, the concept of AI literacy in language education remains fragmented across disciplines and lacks a comprehensive synthesis of its global development. This study therefore investigates research trends, intellectual structures, emerging themes, and future directions in AI literacy within language education. A systematic literature review integrated with bibliometric analysis was employed using 198 Scopus-indexed publications retrieved in April 2026. Data were analyzed through VOSviewer using publication trend analysis, keyword co-occurrence mapping, overlay visualization, and density visualization. The findings reveal a sharp rise in publication output after 2024, indicating growing scholarly attention following the diffusion of generative AI technologies. Thematic mapping identified four dominant knowledge clusters: teacher readiness and professional development, AI-assisted language learning, generative AI applications in EFL/ESL contexts, and critical AI literacy related to ethics and learner autonomy. Overlay analysis further demonstrates a transition from early tool-adoption studies toward more recent concerns with engagement, pedagogical integration, and responsible AI use. Density analysis shows that while AI literacy and generative AI dominate the literature, assessment models, multilingual contexts, and longitudinal intervention studies remain underdeveloped. The study concludes that AI literacy has evolved into a multidimensional competence central to future language education. These findings provide practical guidance for curriculum design, teacher preparation, and policy development, while offering a research agenda for more inclusive and evidence-based AI integration in language learning.

title: A Smart Decision Support Framework: Leveraging AI and Business Intelligence for Sustainable Higher Education
source_name: International Journal of Management and Data Intelligence
keywords: decision support system|higher education sustainability|sustainability management|business intelligence|artificial intelligence|predictive analytics|natural language processing|automated data extraction|sustainability reporting|university management system|data interoperability|ethical AI|data-driven decision making|resource utilization (natural resources)
abstract: The sustainability management in higher education has become a great challenge as the data is located in various systems and only limited decision-making and support capabilities are available. The data- based decision-making, predictive analytics, and the automation that are AI and BI-based (artificial intelligence and business intelligence) do bring in a very different approach to the problems. This paper argues that smarter decision support systems that are developed through the combination of the cognitive abilities of AI with the structured data processing of BI will amplify most of those management functions. The model uses machine learning algorithms for predictive modelling, natural language processing for automated data extraction, and interactive BI dashboards for real-time analytics. The universities, with the help of the AI-generated wisdom, could do better in their resources utilization, there can also be bettered policies, and last but not least, errors in sustainability reporting could be reduced. This way, it is also a means to solve the problem of compatibility through the more traditional university management systems by using standardized data formats and API-based solutions. Furthermore, the framework follows ethical AI principles such as fairness, transparency, and accountability to ensure the quality of sustainability decision-making. The use of the framework will cause the universities to change their management systems from reactive ones to proactive, data- driven, and thus will become more environmentally friendly and operationally efficient. However, the suggested framework may serve as a scalable and adaptable solution for sustainable higher education although it has some problems such as potential data privacy risks, limitations of the infrastructure, and resistance to technological change. It is proposed that future research should concentrate on perfecting AI models, improving interoperability with legacy systems, and researching on artificial intelligence for a comprehensive sustainability management.

title: AI- vs Human-Based Assessment of Medical Interview Transcripts in a Generative AI–Simulated Patient System: Cross-Sectional Validation Study
topic: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
keywords: AI-assisted assessment|clinical interviewing skills|virtual patients|generative AI|GPT-4|GPT-5|medical education|assessment agreement|evaluation time|clinical instructors|medical students|residents (medical training)|attending physicians|rubric-based assessment|reliability statistics|musculoskeletal examination
abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in medical education, including AI-based virtual patients to improve interview skills. However, how much AI-based assessment (ABA) differs from human-based assessment (HBA) remains unclear. Objective: This study aimed to compare the quality of clinical interview assessments generated via an ABA (GPT-o1 Pro [ABA-o1] and GPT-5 Pro [ABA-5]) with those generated via an HBA conducted by clinical instructors in an AI-based virtual patient setting. We also examined whether AI reduced evaluation time and assessed agreement across participants with different levels of clinical experience. Methods: A standardized case of leg weakness was implemented in an AI-based virtual patient. Seven participants (2 medical students, 3 residents, and 2 attending physicians) each conducted an interview with the AI patient, and transcripts were scored using the 25-item Master Interview Rating Scale (0-125). Three evaluation strategies were compared. First, GPT-o1 Pro and GPT-5 Pro scored each transcript 5 times with different random seeds to test case specificity. Processing time was logged automatically. Second, 5 blinded clinical instructors independently rated each transcript once using the same rubric. Third, reliability metrics were applied. For AI, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) quantified repeatability. For humans, the ICC(2,1) was calculated. Agreement was quantified using the Pearson r, Lin concordance correlation coefficient, Bland-Altman limits of agreement, Cronbach α, and ICC. Time efficiency was expressed as mean minutes per transcript and relative percentage reduction. Results: Mean interview scores were similar across methods (ABA-o1: mean 52.1, SD 6.9; ABA-5: mean 53.2, SD 6.8; HBA: mean 53.7, SD 6.8). Agreement between ABA and HBA was strong (r=0.90; concordance correlation coefficient=0.88) with minimal bias (ABA-o1: mean 0.4, SD 2.7; ABA-5: mean 1.5, SD 5.2; limits of agreement: -4.9 to 5.7 for ABA-o1 and -8.6 to 11.7 for ABA-5). The Cronbach α was 0.81 (ABA-o1), 0.86 (ABA-5), and 0.80 (HBA); the ICC(3,1) was 0.77 (ABA-o1) and 0.82 (ABA-5); and the ICC(2,1) was 0.38 (HBA). The coefficient of variation for ABA was approximately half that of HBA (6.6% vs 13.9%). Processing time for 5 runs was 4 minutes, 19 seconds for ABA-o1 and 3 minutes, 20 seconds for ABA-5 vs 10 minutes, 16 seconds for physicians, corresponding to 58% and 67.6% reductions, respectively. Conclusions: ABA-o1 and ABA-5 produced scores closely matching HBA while demonstrating superior consistency and reliability. In the setting of virtual interview transcripts, these findings suggest that ABA may serve as a valid, rapid, and scalable alternative to HBA, reducing per-assessment time by over half. Applied strategically, AI-based scoring could enable timely feedback, improve efficiency, and reduce faculty workload. Further research is needed to confirm generalizability across broader settings.

title: Reliability of ChatGPT answers to common questions on developmental dysplasia of the hip as an information source for parents
topic: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
keywords: ChatGPT|large language models|artificial intelligence|developmental dysplasia of the hip|parental education|patient information resources|frequently asked questions|pediatric orthopedics|GPT-4o
abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly AI-based large language models (LLM) like ChatGPT, is increasingly shaping how information is accessed, offering patients a new source for understanding complex medical conditions. Given the physical, emotional, and logistical challenges that parents are faced when their baby is diagnosed with developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), the demand for clear and accessible educational resources is high. This study aimed to evaluate the quality and reliability of ChatGPT's responses to frequently asked questions about DDH. Methods: This study assessed the quality of responses generated by the AI chatbot ChatGPT 4o to eight frequently asked questions about DDH, derived from real consultations in a pediatric orthopedic clinic Responses were generated during one interaction per question using a ChatGPT account not previously exposed to medical information. Responses were evaluated by two individual readers using a standardized rating system, comparing them to current literature, patient education resources, and consensus guidelines. Each response was categorized by its level of informational accuracy and completeness, and descriptive statistics were calculated to quantify performance. Results: ChatGPT 4o was able to generate structured responses to all eight parental questions. The responses were rated in 12.5% excellent, 25.0% satisfactory with minimal clarification, 50.0% satisfactory with moderate clarification, and 12.5% unsatisfactory due to missing or inaccurate information. Conclusion: ChatGPT provided satisfactory answers to questions about DDH and may serve as a useful supplementary information resource for parents. However, due to limitations in presenting detailed diagnostic and treatment pathways, it should be viewed as an adjunct to, not a replacement for, specialist medical consultation.

title: Integrating Exploratory Data Analysis and Explainable AI into Astronomy Education: A Fuzzy Approach to Data-Literate Learning
keywords: astronomy education|exploratory data analysis|explainable AI|fuzzy logic|fuzzy clustering|data literacy|project-based learning|Gaia DR3|JPL Horizons|stellar classification|orbital structure|reproducible research|STEM education
abstract: Astronomy provides an exceptional context for developing data literacy, critical thinking, and computational skills in education. This paper presents a project-based learning (PBL) framework that integrates exploratory data analysis (EDA), fuzzy logic, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to teach students how to extract and interpret scientific knowledge from real astronomical data. Using open-access resources such as NASA’s JPL Horizons and ESA’s Gaia DR3, together with Python libraries like Astroquery and Plotly, learners retrieve, process, and visualize dynamic datasets of comets, asteroids, and stars. The methodology follows the full data science pipeline, from acquisition and preprocessing to modeling and interpretation, culminating with the application of the FAS-XAI framework (Fuzzy-Adaptive System for Explainable AI) for pattern discovery and interpretability. Through this approach, students can reproduce astronomical analyses and understand how data-driven methods reveal underlying physical relationships, such as orbital structures and stellar classifications. The results demonstrate that combining EDA with fuzzy clustering and explainable models promotes deeper conceptual understanding and analytical reasoning. From an educational perspective, this experience highlights how inquiry-based and computationally rich activities can bridge the gap between theoretical astronomy and data science, empowering students to see the Universe as a laboratory for exploration, reasoning, and discovery. This framework thus provides an effective model for incorporating artificial intelligence, open data, and reproducible research practices into STEM education.

title: Child-centered integration of generative AI in early learning: balancing promises and challenges
keywords: generative AI|early childhood education|developmental appropriateness|AI ethics|algorithmic bias|play-based learning|personalized learning|educational equity|teacher professional development|sociocultural theory|AI regulation|culturally responsive curriculum
abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming educational contexts, yet its role in early childhood education (ECE) raises complex issues regarding developmental appropriateness, ethics, and equity. ECE deserves special attention because it represents a uniquely sensitive and formative stage of human development. This conceptual paper examines the promises and challenges of integrating GenAI into early learning environments, emphasizing both opportunities for innovation and the need for critical safeguards. The discussion highlights potential benefits, including personalized and adaptive learning, enhanced multimodal storytelling, support for play-based pedagogy, and teacher workload reduction. These opportunities, however, are moderated by challenges and risks such as overreliance on screen-based interactions, displacement of play and social relationships, inequitable access, algorithmic bias, and threats to children’s privacy and safety. To address these tensions, the paper situates GenAI within developmental psychology, sociocultural learning theory, educational technology frameworks, and ethical paradigms. Policy and practice implications are outlined, stressing the importance of regulation, equity-focused infrastructure, teacher professional development, and culturally responsive curriculum design. The paper concludes with recommendations for educators, policymakers, and researchers, and introduces a conceptual framework for “Child-Centered GenAI Integration,” arguing that developmental appropriateness, ethical safeguards, and sociocultural mediation must work together to ensure child-centered GenAI use in ECE.

title: Integrarea instrumentelor IA în predarea RLS
keywords: generative AI|Romanian as a foreign language|artificial intelligence in language teaching|ChatGPT|Gemini|lesson planning|educational content development|teacher feedback|inductive method|communicative language teaching
abstract: The evolution of foreign language teaching methodologies has marked a historical transition from approaches based on grammar and translation, towards communicative and direct methods, prioritising oral competences and an inductive approach (widely accepted in foreign language teaching literature as the golden standard). Based on this dynamic process, this article analyses the role and integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) in teaching, with specific focus on teaching Romanian as a foreign language. The purpose of this paper is thus to define the key concepts and to identify practical solutions offered by tools such as ChatGPT or Gemini to generate educational content. Scrutinising recent literature (à la Morehouse and Wong 2025), this article explores the way in which Gen AI can assist teachers in lesson planning, content creation, evaluation and feedback, emphasising the unprecedented amplitude of these digital resources.

title: AI-Powered Generation of Teaching Materials to Support Autonomous Learning in Higher Education
source_name: Journal of Higher Education Theory and Practice
keywords: generative AI|self-directed learning|large language models|bilingual corpus|olive pomace|content validation|responsible AI use|higher education
abstract: This study presents and evaluates an automated system for generating personalized lecture notes through artificial intelligence, designed to foster autonomous learning in higher education. A modular Python-based workflow integrating local large language models (LLMs) processed a bilingual corpus (Spanish– English) to extract, synthesize, and validate content. Five progressively broader queries—ranging from the definition and composition of olive pomace to its production, industrial uses, and environmental challenges—were tested under two conditions: closed mode (local sources) and open mode (including online references). The system produced coherent notes covering around 90% of key concepts, consistently citing references, with external sources enriching content without reducing coherence. Quantitative evaluation showed keyword coverage of 85–95%, strong agreement between automatic validation and experts (κ=0.85), excellent inter-rater reliability (ICC=0.92), and processing times of about 15 seconds. Results highlight the pedagogical potential, efficiency gains, and ethical challenges of integrating generative AI responsibly in higher education.

title: On emerging paradigm of teaching measurement science and technology in times of ubiquitous use of AI tools
keywords: artificial intelligence in higher education|AI tools in teaching|curriculum modernization|autonomous vehicles|social robots|biomedical engineering|automated manufacturing
abstract: The ubiquitous use of the tools of artificial intelligence (AI) in techno-science, in higher education and in other existing and potential fields of measurement application generates new challenges for teaching measurement science and technology (MST). The aim of this article is to encourage its readers to modernize their approach to teaching MST in a way as to meet these challenges, in particular - to profit from new technological opportunities, and to respond to the needs of our civilization, identified within a humanistic reflection over its development. First, the state of the art in applications of AI in higher education is briefly characterized. Next, a methodology for using AI tools in MST, referring to the author's meta-model of measurement, is outlined. Finally, conclusions concerning an emerging paradigm of teaching MST are summarized. The most important of them are as follows. The challenges implied by the ubiquitous use of AI tools cannot be effectively faced without enhancing, in the corresponding curricula, of the contents related to mathematical modelling of material entities, on the one hand, and of the contents related to ethics of research and engineering, on the other. Knowledge and skills related to the art of mathematical modelling are indispensable for extensively profiting from the convergence of various technologies around IT tools, including AI tools. The knowledge and skills related to ethics of research and engineering are indispensable for developing safe applications of measurement in such domains as autonomous vehicles, social robots, biomedical engineering or automated manufacturing.

title: Application Possibilities Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Physical Education
keywords: teacher perceptions|physical education teachers|primary school teachers|preschool teachers|skill development|data collection|teacher technological competence
abstract: In our research, our aim was to examine the opinions of educators (elementary school teachers, preschool teachers, and physical education teachers) regarding the potential applications of artificial intelligence (AI). Our goal was to explore how the surveyed educators perceive AI in relation to physical education, and in which areas professionals believe it could be applied in their own work during physical education sessions. We used a questionnaire-based method in our research. A total of 383 individuals participated in the study. The sample (N=383) consisted of 33.15% elementary and preschool teachers and 66.84% physical education teachers. The results indicated that the participants of the research saw the greatest significance of AI use in data collection, skill development, and the implementation of individualized development programs. Artificial intelligence can support the work of teachers in many ways. However, teachers must also understand the potential of AI and how to use it. We agree with authors such as Hyun and Junga (2021) and Fatih (2025), who emphasize that future physical education teachers must possess technological and AI expertise to effectively integrate AI tools.

title: Embedding-Based Rankings of Educational Resources based on Learning Outcome Alignment: Benchmarking, Expert Validation, and Learner Performance
keywords: text embeddings|large language models|personalized learning|learner performance|expert validation|online learning
abstract: As the online learning landscape evolves, the need for personalization is increasingly evident. Although educational resources are burgeoning, educators face challenges selecting materials that both align with intended learning outcomes and address diverse learner needs. Large Language Models (LLMs) are attracting growing interest for their potential to create learning resources that better support personalization, but verifying coverage of intended outcomes still requires human alignment review, which is costly and limits scalability. We propose a framework that supports the cost-effective automation of evaluating alignment between educational resources and intended learning outcomes. Using human-generated materials, we benchmarked LLM-based text-embedding models and found that the most accurate model (Voyage) achieved 79% accuracy in detecting alignment. We then applied the optimal model to LLM-generated resources and, via expert evaluation, confirmed that it reliably assessed correspondence to intended outcomes (83% accuracy). Finally, in a three-group experiment with 360 learners, higher alignment scores were positively related to greater learning performance, chi-squared(2, N = 360) = 15.39, p < 0.001. These findings show that embedding-based alignment scores can facilitate scalable personalization by confirming alignment with learning outcomes, which allows teachers to focus on tailoring content to diverse learner needs.

title: Investigating Artificial Intelligence Anxiety among University Students in Northern Cyprus
source_name: Cyprus Turkish Journal of Psychiatry and Psychology
keywords: AI anxiety|university students|artificial intelligence in education|gender differences|age differences|Northern Cyprus
abstract: Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into daily life is becoming widespread in various sectors, especially education, and this increases concerns about artificial intelligence among university students. The current study aims to investigate AI anxiety among university students in northern Cyprus in terms of how prevalent or varied it is according to selected demographic and experiential factors. AI anxiety scale was used to measure students’ anxiety along four dimensions: Learning, AI Configuration, Job Replacement, and Sociotechnical Blindness. Data (n=395) were collected from university students in Northern Cyprus and analyzed using Mann-Whitney U tests and Kruskal-Wallis H tests. Findings show that students experienced the highest anxiety at job replacement (Mean = 3.42, SD = 0.82) and the lowest at learning (Mean = 2.91, SD = 1.06). Non-STEM students experienced significantly higher levels of AI anxiety than their STEM students (p <0.001), while females exhibited higher levels than males (p <0.001). Additionally, students with over five hours of use of the technology per day demonstrated the highest anxiety levels (p = 0.013). Age differences were significant, too, with the highest level of anxiety toward AI reported among 21–23-year-old students (p = 0.014). Based on these results, awareness-raising activities and guidance services regarding the use of artificial intelligence can help students better understand this technology and manage their anxiety. In addition, to reduce the AI ​​anxiety experienced by students during this technological transformation process, it will be useful to develop strategies suitable for the needs of different demographic and academic groups and organize awareness-raising and training programs.

title: AI-Powered Tutors as a Catalyst for Conceptual Understanding in Einsteinian Physics Education
topic: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
keywords: conceptual change theory|spacetime curvature|time dilation|Bayesian Knowledge Tracing|cognitive load|virtual simulation|metacognition|inquiry-based learning|personalized feedback
abstract: Purpose of the study: The objective of this study is to investigate the role of AI-powered tutors in assisting students to rectify Newtonian misconceptions and attain a conceptual comprehension of Einsteinian physics concepts, including spacetime curvature, time dilation, and gravity as geometry. Methodology: A conceptual and narrative literature review was performed utilizing databases such as Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar. The utilized tools and frameworks encompass conceptual change theory, constructivism, cognitive load theory, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, reinforcement learning, virtual simulations, and natural language processing. Main Findings: AI-driven tutors proficiently identify misconceptions, deliver tailored feedback, and present multimodal simulations of relativistic phenomena. They augment conceptual comprehension, diminish cognitive load, elevate student engagement and motivation, and facilitate inquiry-based learning. Recently researches indicates enhanced conceptual precision and acceptance of Einsteinian models when artificial intelligence is incorporated with guided instruction. Novelty/Originality of this study: This study integrates artificial intelligence technologies with conceptual change theory and Einsteinian physics education to propose a systematic pedagogical framework. It enhances understanding by demonstrating how AI operates as a cognitive collaborator, improving conceptual restructuring, metacognition, and accessibility to contemporary physics instead of supplanting educators.
